About: Capacitors in Series and Parallel

Source

Topic
Electrostatics — capacitor networks
Concept
Capacitors in series give LESS than either one alone — the exact opposite of what the same word does to resistors.
Level
NCERT Class 12 / JEE Physics
Misconception
"Series adds, like resistors." For capacitors, parallel adds directly (C₁+C₂) and series adds reciprocally (1/C₁+1/C₂).

Guided Inquiry

1 · Predict, before you connect

You have two capacitors, C₁ and C₂, and a battery. You will wire them across the SAME supply two ways: in series, and in parallel. Which network draws more total charge from the supply?

2 · Watch the plates fill

Press ▶ Play. Both networks charge up from the same battery. Watch the +Q shading fill each capacitor.

Notice the geometry the drawing makes literal:

• On the LEFT (series), the two capacitors stack — the effective gap grows. Bigger gap ⇒ smaller C.
• On the RIGHT (parallel), the plates sit side by side — the effective plate area grows. Bigger area ⇒ bigger C.

The Q bars fill as the plates do, on one shared scale — parallel ends far higher.

3 · Verify what you saw

With the defaults (C₁ = 2 µF, C₂ = 3 µF), the series network's effective capacitance is 1.2 µF. Compare that to C₁ and C₂ themselves. What is true?

4 · Which quantity is SHARED?

Two more rules that the picture also tells you:

• In series, both carry the SAME CHARGE and SPLIT the voltage — one path, one flow of charge.
• In parallel, both carry the SAME VOLTAGE and SPLIT the charge — wired to the same two nodes.

Both are on screen: V₁ + V₂ = the supply voltage; Q₁ + Q₂ = the charge delivered.

Push C₂ up. Parallel grows one-for-one; series saturates at C₁ — never more than the smaller capacitor.

5 · The one thing to remember

Capacitors are the opposite way round from resistors.

• Resistors: series ADDS, parallel is reciprocal.
• Capacitors: parallel ADDS, series is reciprocal.

So the reflex "series adds" is a trap here — and knowing the resistor case makes the mistake MORE likely, not less. When you next see a capacitor network, ask first: which way round am I?

The Physics

Capacitors: Series vs Parallel · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

The same two capacitors are wired to one supply in two ways at once, end to end on the left and side by side on the right, and the sim charges both so you can compare them. Circuit designers make this choice when they need a particular capacitance or voltage rating.

What you'll learn

  • How the effective capacitance of a pair of capacitors depends on how they are wired.
  • Which quantity, charge or voltage, the two capacitors share in each wiring, and which one they split.
  • How to find the charge and the energy a network takes from a supply, using Q = CV and U = ½CV².
The same two capacitors on one supply V: stacked in a single loop on the left, side by side on the right.

What's on screen

  • Series network (left, pink): the battery with C₁ and C₂ stacked in one loop, labelled with the voltage each holds.
  • Parallel network (right, blue): C₁ and C₂ side by side across the same two rails, labelled with the charge each holds.
  • Plates: amber is the + plate and cyan the − plate. The shading between them grows as a capacitor charges.
  • Bars (bottom): charge Q and energy U for each network, all four on one scale.
  • Effective capacitance panel (sidebar): Cₛ and Cₚ for the current C₁ and C₂.
See itPress Play with C₁ = 2 µF, C₂ = 3 µF and V = 12 V. Watch for: the plates in both columns filling with charge, and the four bars at the bottom rising together.

03

Capacitors in parallel add directly

In parallel, both capacitors connect to the same two rails, so each has the full supply voltage V across it. Each stores its own charge, Q₁ = C₁V and Q₂ = C₂V, and the supply delivers the sum Q = (C₁ + C₂)V. The pair therefore acts as one capacitor:

Cₚ = C₁ + C₂
Same voltage on both, and the charge splits in proportion to C.

The drawing makes the reason literal: side by side, the plates add their areas, A₁ + A₂, and more plate area means more capacitance. With C₁ = 2 µF, C₂ = 3 µF and V = 12 V, Cₚ = 5 µF. The charges are Q₁ = 24 µC and Q₂ = 36 µC, and the supply delivers 60 µC in all. Cₚ is bigger than either capacitor alone.

See itCharge the defaults and read the labels above the parallel plates. Watch for: Q₁ and Q₂ above the plates climbing to 24.00 µC and 36.00 µC, and Cₚ = 5.00 µF in the panel.
04

Capacitors in series add as reciprocals

In series there is one path, and the capacitors start uncharged, so the same charge Q ends up on each. The supply voltage splits: V = V₁ + V₂ = Q/C₁ + Q/C₂ = Q(1/C₁ + 1/C₂). Writing V = Q/Cₛ gives:

1/Cₛ = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂
Same charge on both, and the voltage splits in inverse proportion to C.

For two capacitors this is Cₛ = C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂). The drawing stacks the gaps, so the effective gap is d₁ + d₂, and a bigger gap means a smaller capacitance. For 2 µF and 3 µF, Cₛ = 6/5 = 1.2 µF. The same Q = 14.4 µC sits on both, and the voltages are V₁ = Q/C₁ = 7.2 V and V₂ = Q/C₂ = 4.8 V, which add to 12 V. The smaller capacitor holds the larger share.

See itCharge the defaults and read the labels beside the stacked capacitors. Watch for: V₁ and V₂ settling at 7.20 V and 4.80 V, adding to the 12 V supply, with one shared Q = 14.40 µC.
05

A series pair stays below its smaller capacitor

Because Cₛ = C₁ · C₂/(C₁ + C₂) and the fraction C₂/(C₁ + C₂) is always less than 1, Cₛ is less than C₁. The same argument gives Cₛ less than C₂. So a series pair is smaller than the smaller of the two. With C₁ = 2 µF the partner changes Cₛ like this:

C₂CₛCₚ
1 µF0.67 µF3 µF
3 µF1.20 µF5 µF
6 µF1.50 µF8 µF

Even a 6 µF partner lifts Cₛ only to 1.5 µF. A much larger partner would push Cₛ toward 2 µF without ever reaching it. Two equal capacitors C in series give C/2, and every extra capacitor in series adds another term to 1/Cₛ, so it lowers Cₛ again.

See itKeep C₁ = 2 µF and raise C₂ to 6 µF. Watch for: Cₛ = 1.50 µF, still below C₁ = 2.0 µF, while Cₚ = 8.00 µF.
06

Charge and energy follow the supply voltage

Either network acts as one capacitor C across the supply, so the charge it draws and the energy it stores are

Q = CV,   U = ½CV²
C is Cₛ or Cₚ, whichever network you are reading.

At fixed capacitances, doubling V doubles Q and quadruples U. Both networks see the same V, so the parallel-to-series ratio of charge, and of energy, equals Cₚ/Cₛ. For the defaults it is 5/1.2, about 4.2. At 24 V the series network holds 28.8 µC and 345.6 µJ, and the parallel network 120 µC and 1.44 mJ. The bars share one scale whose full height is the parallel network at 24 V. The plates fill at a fixed rate on screen, which says nothing about how long a real capacitor takes to charge.

C₁ C₂ V

See itRaise the supply to 24 V with the default capacitors. Watch for: the parallel Q and U bars reaching full height, with Q = 120.00 µC and U = 1.44 mJ.
07

Where it matters

  • Making a value. Parallel adds capacitance from the parts you have: 2 µF and 3 µF make 5 µF. Series reaches a smaller value: two 10 µF capacitors make 5 µF.
  • Sharing a high voltage. A series stack splits the supply, so each capacitor sees only part of it. Two equal capacitors share it equally, at the cost of half the capacitance. Unequal ones do not: the smaller capacitor takes the larger share, so it is the one at risk of overload.
  • Storing energy. A bank of capacitors in parallel stores U = ½CₚV² at the supply voltage, so adding capacitors adds energy. Large capacitor banks are built this way.
  • A mirror of resistors. The two rules are the resistor rules with series and parallel swapped.
08

Summary

In one line. How two capacitors are wired sets their effective capacitance, and that sets the charge and energy the network takes from the supply.

Key points

  • Parallel: same V on both, Cₚ = C₁ + C₂.
  • Series: same Q on both, 1/Cₛ = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂.
  • For either network, Q = CV and U = ½CV².

Common mix-ups

  • "Series adds, as it does for resistors." For capacitors the rules swap: parallel adds directly, and series adds as reciprocals.
  • "Each series capacitor has the full supply voltage across it." They share the supply, V₁ + V₂ = V. Each carries the same charge.
  • "Parallel capacitors hold the same charge." They hold the same voltage. The charge splits in proportion to C, equal only when C₁ = C₂.

Things to try on your own

  • Find C₁ and C₂ that give Cₚ = 4 µF and Cₛ = 0.75 µF, then set them and check both readouts.
  • Set C₁ = C₂ = 4 µF and compare Cₛ and Cₚ with 4 µF.
  • For the default capacitors at V = 20 V, work out Qₚ and Uₚ, then compare with the parallel bars.
